title: Architecture & Standards: API, Code, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards for API design, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also defines the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process used for making and recording long-lived architectural choices. The intent is to provide a single reference teams can use to design new services, onboard models, and evaluate changes to production systems.

Audience
- Engineers (backend, runtime, infra, SRE)
- Product and platform owners
- Security and compliance reviewers

Key principles
- Developer-first: standards favor clear ergonomics and fast iteration while preserving safety for production workloads.
- Production-grade: every service must meet reliability, performance, and cost targets appropriate to its tier.
- Observable and debuggable: design for high signal observability (metrics, traces, logs) by default.
- Explicit decisions: major architecture choices are recorded as ADRs.

1) API Standards
Purpose: Provide consistent, stable, and backward-compatible APIs for client integrations, SDKs, and internal services.

Must-have rules
- Use OpenAPI 3.1 for all public and internal HTTP APIs. Publish the spec in the repo root under /api/openapi.yaml and link it from docs-site.
- Versioning: follow semantic versioning for API surfaces (v{major}.{minor}) in the path, e.g. /v1/models/{id}/generate. Breaking changes require a major version bump and a migration guide.
- Request/response format: JSON default. Use UTF-8 and follow RFC 8259.
- Error model: standardize on an error envelope: {"code": string, "message": string, "request_id": string}. HTTP status codes must be correct (4xx client, 5xx server).
- Idempotency: POST endpoints that create resources must accept an Idempotency-Key header and be idempotent for 24 hours.
- Pagination: use cursor-based pagination for large result sets: {"next_cursor": string, "items": []}.
- Streaming: use chunked transfer encoding or server-sent events for streaming responses; provide an equivalent non-streaming endpoint.
- Authentication: bearer token (Authorization: Bearer <token>) for API access; rotate keys via console.
- Rate limiting and throttling: responses must include X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset headers.

Guidelines and examples
- Model inference endpoints should separate generation parameters (temperature, top_p) from routing hints (region_hint, preferred_variant).
- Example OpenAPI snippet and error envelope included in the API library repo (see /contrib/api-examples).

Ownership: eng-developer-experience + eng-platform maintain the API templates and OpenAPI generator.

2) Coding Standards
Purpose: Ensure maintainable, testable, and secure code across services.

Language and repo rules
- Preferred languages: Go for high-throughput services (runtime, proxies), Python for SDKs and tooling, TypeScript for frontend.
- Monorepo for platform infra and runtime is allowed; service-specific code may be in single-repo per service.
- Naming: use short, descriptive package and service names (kebab-case for repos, camelCase for Go packages).

Quality rules
- Linters: gofmt/golangci-lint for Go, black/ruff/flake8 for Python, eslint/prettier for TS. All CI pipelines must run linters.
- Testing: unit tests required; integration tests required for any change touching API contracts or infra provisioning. Test coverage target: minimum 60% for service code; critical paths >80%.
- Types: prefer explicit types (Go structs, Python pydantic models) for API boundaries.
- Secrets: never commit secrets. Use the secrets manager (Vault/KMS). CI rejects commits with secret patterns.

PR and review process
- PRs must include: description, testing steps, rollout plan (if applicable), and link to the ADR if it implements or modifies an architectural decision.
- Two reviewers required for production-impacting changes.

3) Infrastructure Standards
Purpose: Provide repeatable, auditable, and secure provisioning of cloud and on-prem resources.

Provisioning and IaC
- Terraform for cloud infra (account, VPC, IAM, KMS). Modules live under /infra/terraform-modules and must include examples and tests.
- Cloud accounts: separate accounts per environment (prod, staging, dev). Enforce guardrails via organization policies.
- Networking: services should be deployed in private subnets behind load balancers. Public ingress only through API gateway or dedicated proxy.
- Secrets and keys: KMS for envelope encryption; HSM-backed keys for customer-managed keys (CMKs) for Private deployments.

Naming and tagging
- Standard tags: {project, service, owner, environment, cost_center}. Resources without tags are flagged in cost reviews.

Deployment and rollout
- CI/CD: use standardized pipelines in eng-infra/ci-cd-and-build with required steps: build -> unit tests -> integration tests -> canary deploy -> promote.
- Canary policy: default canary size 5%-10% for 30 minutes with health checks. Canary rollback automatic on failures.

Ownership: eng-infra (Terraform modules), eng-platform (deployment pipelines).

4) Model-Serving Standards
Purpose: Ensure models are served efficiently, safely, and with predictable economics across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private modes.

Model packaging and onboarding
- Model manifest: every model must include a manifest.json with model_id, version, architecture, tokenizer, max_sequence_length, quantization_profile, ABI-compatible runtime (e.g., rtx-v2), owner, and approved_datasets.
- CI checks: validate manifest, run quick smoke-generation tests, and evaluate latency perf-suite for representative prompts.

Runtime and variants
- Runtime variants: define at least three serving variants per model where applicable: fast (FP16, small context), balanced (int8/quantized), and cost-saver (aggressive quantization). Each variant must have a documented performance profile (p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput tokens/s, memory footprint).
- KV cache policy: default to prefix caching for chat sessions; provide TTL and max-entries config per model route.

SLOs and safety
- SLA tiers: Host API default SLO: 99.9% availability; Dedicated SLA negotiated per contract. Hard p99 latency targets are defined per route in the model catalog.
- Safety: model outputs flagged by safety filter must be logged, sampled for review, and optionally routed to a suppression pipeline. See safety-runbook for triage.

Rollouts and fallback
- Rollout: use canary + A/B + automatic fallback to a compatible variant on SLO violations.
- Fallback ordering: identical-architecture quantized -> smaller context fast variant -> canonical cloud model.

Ownership: eng-serving-runtime + applied-ml-and-evals for perf and quality gating.

5) Observability Standards
Purpose: Make system behavior visible at token, request, and service levels to enable rapid debugging and cost optimization.

Telemetry requirements
- Metrics: export metrics using OpenTelemetry. Required metrics for model-serving endpoints: request_count, request_success_count, request_error_count, request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), tokens_generated, cache_hit_rate, model_memory_bytes, gpu_utilization_percent.
- Tracing: instrument RPC boundaries and model inference spans. Include request_id and user_id where permitted. Sample rate: 1% by default; adjustable per-service.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with keys: timestamp, level, request_id, span_id, service, operation, error (if any), and additional context. Logs must be forwarded to the central ELK/observability cluster with 30-day hot retention for prod by default.

Dashboards and alerts
- Dashboards: every service must ship a dashboard template with: latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, throughput, cost/token, and key resource usage (CPU, GPU, memory). Use the unified dashboard repo under eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts.
- Alerts: standard alert thresholds:
  - error-rate > 0.5% for 10 minutes -> P1 paging to on-call
  - p99 latency > target * 1.5 for 5 minutes -> P1
  - cache_hit_rate drop > 20% over 30 minutes -> P2
  - GPU memory OOM events -> P0
- Alerting workflow: PagerDuty for P0/P1; Slack channel notifications for P2. Runbook links included in alerts.

Cost observability
- Token-level cost attribution: record tokens_generated per request and map to cost center tags. Reports: daily cost aggregation per model route.

Ownership: eng-sre (alerting, runbooks) and eng-platform (dashboards).

6) Performance Standards and Benchmarks
Purpose: Establish measurable performance baselines to guide model selection, kernel choices, and capacity planning.

Benchmarking suite
- Benchmark harness: eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite provides standardized workloads for throughput, latency, and memory profiling. Benchmarks used: short-chat (context < 128 tokens), long-completion (context up to 4k), and embeddings-bulk.
- Reporting: record metrics p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s throughput, and GPU utilization. Store daily runs in perf-store with metadata (model, variant, hardware).

Targets and profiling cadence
- Target latency (hosted defaults): short-chat p99 <= 150ms; long-completion p99 <= 1200ms (depends on length); embeddings p95 <= 50ms for small vectors.
- Profiling cadence: heavy models profiled weekly; new model onboarding runs a full perf-suite and kernel tuning before approving production variant.

Optimization guidance
- Use batching and KV caching to improve throughput while preserving latency SLOs. Default batch size auto-configured by runtime with workload-aware throttling.
- Quantization policy: prefer int8 for balanced variants; aggressive quantization for cost-saver if quality regression < 2% on eval metrics.

Ownership: eng-serving-runtime (bench harness), applied-ml-and-evals (quality regression gating).

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
Purpose: Make architectural decisions explicit, discoverable, and reversible.

Process
1. Problem statement: author creates ADR draft when a decision has system-level impact (cross-team, infra, SLOs, or customer-facing behavior).
2. Alternatives: document considered options and trade-offs.
3. Decision: chosen approach and rationale.
4. Consequences: operational, security, cost, and migration implications.
5. Review and approval: reviewers include owners of impacted subsystems.
6. Publish: ADRs are stored in /docs/adr (repo) and linked from Confluence. Minor changes can be an ADR addendum; major reversals require a new ADR that supersedes the prior one.

Template (fields)
- ADR ID: ADR-YYYY-NNN
- Title
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated
- Date
- Authors
- Context and problem statement
- Decision drivers
- Considered options
- Decision outcome
- Consequences and follow-ups

Sample recent ADRs
- ADR-2025-023: Standardize inference API error envelope (accepted). Reason: unify SDK error handling and simplify client retries. Consequence: existing clients required migration; SDKs provide compatibility shims for 6 months.
- ADR-2025-041: Adopt OpenTelemetry and centralize tracing (accepted). Reason: improve distributed tracing across hosted and private deployments. Consequence: moderate CPU overhead; sampling defaulted to 1%.
- ADR-2026-005: Default model serving variant strategy (accepted). Reason: ensure predictable rollbacks and cost profiles. Consequence: model catalog schema extended and onboarding CI updated.

Lifecycle & ownership
- ADRs are owned by eng-platform for coordination and archived by eng-developer-experience. Each ADR must list impacted owners.

Appendices
A. Common SLO table (example)
| Route type | Availability SLO | Latency p99 target | Error budget |
| Hosted inference (standard) | 99.9% | 150ms (short-chat) / 1200ms (long) | 0.1% monthly |
| Dedicated (contracted) | SLA negotiated | defined per route | contractual |

B. Terraform module checklist
- Module README present
- Examples folder included
- Input and output variables documented
- Tests (unit/integration) exist in CI
- Tagging and naming enforced

C. API change release checklist
1. Update OpenAPI spec and generate client SDKs.
2. Add migration guide and deprecation schedule.
3. Run integration tests against staging.
4. Announce to customers and internal teams.

D. Contact & escalation
- Standards owner: eng-platform (standards@redwood-inference.internal)
- ADR coordinator: Priya Menon (priya@redwood-inference.internal)
- On-call SRE: see eng-sre rota in /oncall-and-incident-response
